source.title: Embracing Anisotropy: Turning Massive Activations into Interpretable Control Knobs for Large Language Models
source.authors: Y. Roh; Hyunjin Cho; Jaehyung Kim

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies hidden-state dimensions, not neuron poles, and does not test any of the listed neuron-specific claim versions. Its discussion of interpretable units and its dimension-level results do not test neuron interpretability or neuron-based attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports masking, token-activation, and steering results for hidden-state dimensions. These are related findings about a different unit, so they are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version; they are not evidence about neuron poles. The dimension steering results also do not test the neuron-based attribution-graph claim.
record.test_reason: The study analyses residual-stream hidden-state dimensions selected by activation magnitude, not MLP neuron poles. It does not audit what share of neurons are interpretable, does not examine InceptionV1, build neuron attribution graphs, or score explanations by simulating activations. Its interpretability analysis covers only top-100 activating tokens for a few hand-picked dimensions, so it cannot bear on V6 or V7. It only touches the topic in passing, acknowledging 'inherent polysemanticity within LLM representations' in its limitations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that magnitude-selected 'Domain-Critical Dimensions' are interpretable functional units, and that steering only those dimensions matches or beats whole-space steering in MMLU domain adaptation and AdvBench jailbreaking. They acknowledge inherent polysemanticity and present SAE-style fine-grained factorization as complementary.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-magnitude selection of hidden-state dimensions, dimension masking, token classification, and activation steering. It does not audit neuron poles or test explanations on held-out activating examples. The paper describes its approach as training-free for dimension selection.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by target domain and selected dimension; domain-adaptation steering tunes dimension count and strength separately by MMLU subject. Jailbreaking results vary with steering strength and dimension count. Token-classification prompts explicitly prioritize domain-specific token classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing one residual dimension at every layer drops MMLU accuracy by up to 14.56 points (Gemma-2-2b-it) and 51.33 points (Qwen-3-8b) at rank 1. Rank-100 drops are small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A few individual residual-stream dimensions are functionally critical for task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Magnitude-selected residual dimensions in Gemma-2 (2b, 9b) and Llama-3.1-8b have top-activating tokens dominated by domain classes in their own domain, per a domain-prioritizing LLM annotator. That specialization disappears in other domains (e.g., dim 1046 is 44% GENERAL in biology).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some high-magnitude residual dimensions act as domain-associated token detectors, in a dataset-dependent way.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The reported dimension findings do not directly measure neuron interpretability. Token-classification analyses use an automated annotator and a prompt that prioritizes domain categories. Domain-adaptation results report the best hyperparameter setting for each subject, and jailbreaking evaluation uses an LLM judge; no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No results directly measuring neuron poles or any listed version were reported. Other dimension-level analyses and per-subject steering values were not separately cataloged because they do not bear on the neuron-specific versions.

untested.parts: Share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one, two or unknown jobs.
Neuron-pole shares across other dense and MoE models and scales.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons such as InceptionV1 cat/car.
Whether architecture, regularization or tools drive neuron interpretability rates.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out text.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The unit studied is the residual hidden-state dimension (massive activations), not MLP neurons, so no row bears on any version. Steering rows r10–r13 are the study's own method performance and should not be result rows. The interpretability evidence is the top-100 activating tokens for hand-picked dimensions, classified by GPT-4o-mini under a prompt instructing it to prioritize domain classes. There are no held-out or simulation tests.

versions.untested_parts: The share of neuron poles with one or more main jobs and the share not understood.
Neuron-pole interpretability across models, architectures, and scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and the proposed interpretation as pose detection or recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain neuron interpretability rates, and the proposed InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons and their ability to explain behavior without replacement-model reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict where neurons fire on unseen activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
